title: IELTS Academic Reading — Practice Test 2
topics: The history and technology of lighthouses

passages.title: Lights Along the Coast: The Making of the Lighthouse

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.html: Long before charts and compasses, sailors navigating unfamiliar coasts relied on landmarks visible from the sea. Where nature provided none, people built their own. The most celebrated of these early markers was the Pharos of Alexandria, raised on an island off the Egyptian coast in the third century BCE and counted among the wonders of the ancient world. By day its tower, said to stand well over a hundred metres, guided vessels toward the harbour; by night a fire kept burning at its summit served the same purpose. Whether the Pharos used mirrors to project its flame, as some later writers claimed, remains uncertain. What is clear is that it fixed in the imagination an idea that would endure for two thousand years: a tall structure crowned with light, warning ships away from danger and drawing them toward safe water.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.html: For most of the centuries that followed, the technology changed little. Coastal communities and, in Europe, religious orders maintained beacons that were essentially open fires, burning wood or coal in iron baskets called chauffers hoisted on towers. Such fires were cheap to build but poor at their task. Wind scattered their light, rain doused them, and on the clearest night their glow faded within a few miles. Worse, an open flame gave no hint of its identity: a mariner who saw a distant light could not tell one headland from another, nor a lighthouse from a bonfire lit by wreckers hoping to lure a ship onto the rocks and plunder its cargo. The central problem of the lighthouse was therefore not merely to produce light but to produce a light that was bright, steady and recognisable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.html: Solving it required advances on two fronts. The first was the source of the light itself. In the eighteenth century, oil lamps with woven wicks replaced open coal fires, giving a cleaner and more controllable flame; the Argand lamp, introduced in the 1780s, added a circular wick and a glass chimney that drew air through the centre, burning brighter than anything before it. The second front was optics. A single lamp, however bright, radiates its light in all directions, wasting most of it on the sky and the ground. Engineers began fitting polished metal reflectors behind their lamps to gather the stray beams and throw them outward toward the horizon. These early reflectors helped, but they were far from efficient, absorbing much of the light they were meant to redirect.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.html: The decisive breakthrough came from France. In 1822 the physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel unveiled a lens unlike any before it. Rather than grinding a single, impossibly thick block of glass, he built up a series of concentric rings, each a precisely angled prism, that bent the scattered rays of a lamp into one concentrated beam. A Fresnel lens could capture the vast majority of a lamp's output and send it many miles out to sea, yet it was lighter and thinner than the solid lens it replaced. Arranged in panels around a rotating frame, such lenses also allowed each station to flash in a distinct rhythm. At last a lighthouse could announce which lighthouse it was, and mariners could match the pattern they saw against the sequence printed on their charts.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.html: Optics were only half the challenge; the other was building at all. The most dangerous hazards to shipping were often not the headlands but the reefs and isolated rocks that lay offshore, submerged at high tide and battered year-round by heavy seas. Erecting a tower on such a site tested the limits of engineering. The Eddystone Rocks, off the southern English coast, defeated two structures before John Smeaton completed a third in 1759. Smeaton modelled his tower on the shape of an oak tree, broad at the base and tapering upward, and secured its granite blocks by cutting them to interlock like the pieces of a puzzle so that the whole mass behaved as a single stone. His design proved so durable that it became the template for wave-swept towers for the next century.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.html: The twentieth century brought electricity, and with it lamps far brighter than any flame, but it also began to make the lighthouse keeper redundant. Automatic timers, remote monitoring and, eventually, solar power meant that stations could run without anyone living in them, and one by one the keepers were withdrawn. The final blow to the lighthouse's old importance came from above. Satellite navigation now allows a ship to fix its position anywhere on earth to within a few metres, without ever sighting the shore. Yet the lighthouses have not gone dark. Electronic systems can fail or be switched off, and a light on a headland offers a simple, independent confirmation that costs a mariner nothing to read. For that reason, and for the powerful hold they retain on public affection, many still turn.

passages.title: Four Days a Week: Rethinking the Shape of Work

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.html: The idea that a full working week should occupy five days is more recent, and more arbitrary, than it seems. For much of the industrial era people laboured six days out of seven; the two-day weekend became standard only in the twentieth century, and largely for practical and commercial reasons rather than any natural law of work. Once that is recognised, the question naturally arises whether the boundary might move again. In recent years, from Iceland to New Zealand, governments, campaign groups and individual firms have run trials of a four-day week, and their results have reignited a debate that touches on economics, wellbeing and the very purpose of paid work.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.html: Supporters make a claim that at first sounds too good to be true: that people can produce as much in four days as in five. The reasoning rests on the observation that time at a desk is a poor measure of useful output. Much of a conventional working week, they argue, is consumed by unnecessary meetings, interruptions and the slow drift of tasks expanding to fill the hours available. Given one fewer day, workers ruthlessly prune the waste — meetings shorten, distractions are refused, and the genuinely productive core of the job is completed in less time. Several trials appear to bear this out, reporting that output held steady or even rose after hours were cut, though critics question how long such gains can last once the novelty fades.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.html: Beyond productivity, advocates point to gains that are harder to measure but no less real. Employees given a third day off report lower stress, better sleep and more time for family, exercise and community life, and firms running trials frequently record sharp falls in sickness absence and in the number of staff resigning. There may be environmental dividends too. A workforce that commutes four days rather than five makes fewer journeys, and offices that close an extra day consume less power on heating, lighting and equipment. Whether these effects are large enough to matter at a national scale is disputed, but the direction of travel, most observers accept, is not seriously in doubt.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.html: Not everyone is convinced, and some of the objections are serious. The clearest is that the four-day week suits some kinds of work far better than others. A software team or a marketing department may well compress its output into fewer hours; a hospital ward, a classroom or a factory production line cannot. Care for patients and teaching of children are measured precisely in the hours devoted to them, and cutting those hours means either hiring more staff, at considerable cost, or delivering less of the service. Sceptics warn that a reform which benefits office workers while leaving front-line staff behind could widen, rather than narrow, existing divisions in the workforce.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.html: Part of the confusion in the debate stems from the fact that 'a four-day week' describes several quite different arrangements. In the version most trials have tested, employees keep their full salary and work roughly eighty per cent of their former hours while committing to maintain their previous output — an approach sometimes summarised as the '100-80-100' model. A second version simply compresses the same total hours into four longer days, leaving pay and workload unchanged but the working day exhausting. A third reduces both hours and pay proportionally. These are not variations on a single policy but genuinely distinct bargains, and evidence gathered about one tells us little about the others.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.html: For employers weighing the change, the calculation is rarely straightforward. Set against the risk of disruption is a powerful advantage in the competition for staff. In a tight labour market, the offer of a three-day weekend can attract applicants that a modest pay rise could not, and firms that have adopted the model report that they retain experienced employees who might otherwise have left. In the largest coordinated trial to date, conducted across dozens of British companies in 2022, the great majority of participating firms chose to continue with the shorter week after the pilot ended. Yet self-selection clouds such findings: the companies willing to run a trial in the first place are unlikely to be a representative sample of the economy as a whole.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.html: Where does this leave the argument? The honest answer is that the four-day week is neither the panacea its enthusiasts describe nor the indulgence its detractors fear. It appears to work well in particular settings — knowledge-based, output-oriented, already reasonably efficient — and poorly in others where the service simply is the time. The more interesting question may not be whether the whole economy should switch to four days, but why the five-day week was ever assumed to be the natural shape of working life. Once that assumption is examined rather than inherited, a wider range of possibilities comes into view.

passages.title: The Words in Our Heads: Does Language Shape Thought?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.html: Consider a simple question: if your language had no word for a particular colour, could you still see it? Or a harder one: does the grammar you absorbed as a child, without ever choosing it, quietly shape the thoughts you are able to think? The proposition that the language we speak influences the way we perceive and reason about the world is known as linguistic relativity. It is an old idea, endlessly appealing and endlessly contested, and for a century it has swung between the poles of scholarly fashion — embraced as a profound truth, dismissed as a seductive error, and, more recently, revived in a chastened and more careful form.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.html: The idea is most closely associated with two American scholars of the early twentieth century, Edward Sapir and his student Benjamin Lee Whorf. Whorf, studying indigenous American languages, became convinced that their grammatical categories — the way they marked time, or divided up events — led their speakers to conceptualise reality along lines quite different from those of European speakers. In its strongest form, the claim became linguistic determinism: the notion that language does not merely influence thought but imprisons it, so that a concept for which one's language has no words is literally unthinkable. It was a bold and thrilling hypothesis, and by the middle of the century it had become widely known well beyond the confines of linguistics.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.html: Then the tide turned decisively against it. Whorf's specific examples were found, on closer inspection, to be exaggerated or simply mistaken. More damaging still was the rise of a rival vision of the mind. Linguists led by Noam Chomsky argued that the deep structure of all human languages is fundamentally the same, an expression of innate mental machinery common to the whole species; the surface differences that so impressed Whorf were, on this account, superficial. A famous study of colour vocabulary seemed to seal the matter. Surveying languages across the world, its authors found that although they carved up the spectrum with different numbers of words, the terms clustered around the same focal shades, suggesting that colour perception was governed by universal biology rather than by the accidents of vocabulary. For a generation, to speak of linguistic relativity was to mark oneself as naive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.html: The idea did not stay buried. From the 1990s a new generation of researchers, armed with experiments rather than anecdotes, began to test far more modest versions of the hypothesis, and some of their findings were striking. The most celebrated concerned an Aboriginal Australian community whose language locates objects not by terms such as 'left' and 'right', which depend on the speaker's own position, but by fixed compass directions — north, south, east and west. To speak the language at all, its users must keep constant track of their orientation, and researchers found that they were correspondingly, almost uncannily, skilled at knowing which way they faced, even in unfamiliar buildings or after being spun around. Here, it seemed, was a habit of language producing a measurable habit of mind.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.html: Other experiments probed subtler effects. Speakers of languages that oblige them to distinguish, say, light blue from dark blue with separate basic words were shown to be slightly faster at telling such shades apart than speakers of languages that use a single word for both — a small but reliable difference, and one that faded when the participants were prevented from using inner speech. Studies of grammatical gender produced results that were suggestive if less conclusive: asked to describe a bridge, speakers of a language in which the word is grammatically feminine tended to reach for adjectives like 'elegant' or 'slender', while speakers of a language that treats it as masculine favoured 'strong' or 'sturdy'. The influence of language, such work implied, was real but limited, operating at the margins of perception and judgement rather than dictating them wholesale.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.html: Critics remained unpersuaded that these effects amounted to much. Correlation, they cautioned, is not causation: a community's remarkable sense of direction might owe more to a life spent navigating open country than to the grammar it happens to use, and the two are hard to disentangle. More fundamentally, the very fact that such experiments can be described, understood and replicated across languages seemed to them to undercut the strong thesis. If speakers of one language were truly imprisoned within its categories, how could a concept from another language ever be explained to them? The everyday reality of translation, imperfect but serviceable, suggests that no linguistic wall is unscalable, and that whatever influence language exerts stops well short of a cage.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.html: Where the debate has settled — insofar as it has settled at all — is on a position that would have satisfied neither Whorf nor his fiercest opponents. Language is now widely seen as one influence among many on thought, capable of nudging attention, easing some mental operations and complicating others, but neither determining what can be thought nor irrelevant to it. What makes the question so durable is that it resists the clean experiment. Thought cannot be observed directly, only inferred from behaviour and, awkwardly, from language itself; to test whether words shape thinking, researchers must in the end rely on the very medium under suspicion. That circularity, more than any shortage of evidence, may be why linguistic relativity, more than most scientific questions, seems destined to be perpetually reopened by each new generation rather than conclusively resolved.
